fullPassage:
The following speech is adapted from a lecture series delivered by Joanne Lesley Malone, a British perfumer. She tells the story of her struggles and successes. My name is Joanne Lesley Malone. I am an entrepreneur, perfumer, and a storyteller with scent. Today I'm going to tell you about the first brand I ever created and all the fun adventures that we had in building a global brand. Everybody faces challenges in life regardless of who you are or where you came from. My dyslexia was certainly a challenge in my life. One of the things I learned as a child at school was that I was struggling to read. I couldn't learn in the same way other children did. I had to think differently and always find a way of getting out of the situations. I would just memorize everything. I have a photographic memory, and I have a very good sense of smell. Those are the two gifts I need. I trust those two things every time I create anything. I started my first brand from my tiny little apartment. I think the very very first note I made was a wild strawberry note and violet. It didn't smell as good as I wanted it to, so I would take it, you know almost like playing the piano, add notes in, take notes out, give a beat to the fragrance, and find it. And I created a wonderful wild strawberry note from that. The fragrances that I created, I would just make by hand and I would sell them to my consumers that would come to have their faces done because I was a beautician in the very beginning. Everybody loved the product, and there was this buzz about everything that we did. And one lady one day bought one-hundred bottles of perfume. It was amazing. Those bottles sat at a place at a party that she was holding. Within one month, eighty-six out of one-hundred people were desperate to buy the product. They thought it was a really big full-on brand, but it wasn't. It was all being made in my kitchen with poor plastic jugs, a little saucepan, and a whole heap of dreams. Those one-hundred people grew and grew and grew until the point where my husband Gary and I, who were business partners as well as best friends, decided to open our first little shop on 154 Walton Street, London. So from day one of opening, we saw everybody was totally captivated by the products that we were creating. And every day I would sit and I would look at the figures that we were bringing in. Not one day did we drop below the previous day. It was an incredible moment of growth. I didn't just take nice neat little fragrances and put them in a bottle and expect it to sell. I took things that collided. I took things that were aggressive and then soft all at the same time, and it worked. It captivated and really challenged people's creativity. Our first global journey from my first brand was to go into the United States. It was so scary. Honestly, I didn't know how on earth we were going to get there. I said to Gary, "How much money do I have for marketing and PR?" "Mm, nothing." There was no money left. We put every single penny we had into our business. "What am I going to do? How am I going to convince everyone to come and buy my product?" He was standing in the corner of the hotel room packing boxes. He started to put bags together and put ribbons around them. I said, "What are you doing that for? There's nothing in there." "No one else knows that." From that day, we employed twenty to thirty people, and they carried hundreds of those empty bags with our logo around New York City. By the time we opened on the first of October, everyone assumed this brand was everywhere. We converted New York City and America—eventually the rest of the world—with people just holding empty bags. As an entrepreneur, such a good lesson. Remember, you can often have the greatest idea that costs pennies but can transform your business into a global market. Our business was growing and growing. I just had a little boy. I was just thirty-eight years old. But you know something? In life sometimes you get curveballs. Mine was about to come from a direction I didn't anticipate. I was diagnosed with breast cancer, and I was given nine months to live. I looked at my son. I wondered if I'd ever see him grow up. Was I going to last for nine months? Well, you can see the evidence sitting before you. What I did realize was I had a chance of getting my life back. What I didn't realize, it would take my sense of smell. I never told a soul. Back to work, back to the shop. But I knew something deep within me had gone. I was "just Jo." I made the decision within a few months that I was to leave the business. You can imagine this emotional connection that I had with my business. It wasn't just a brand to me. It was my life. It was my best friend. As we came to that last week of signing the deal, I felt I'd made the biggest mistake of my life. "What had I done?" This business entrepreneur within me was nearly bursting out, saying, "Please stop. I've made a mistake. I want to go back." But I didn't. I didn't go near any department store, any fragrance shop, anything for five years because it absolutely broke me inside that I had made a huge mistake. I didn't think I would ever enter back into the fragrance industry. But, boy, was it calling me, and I missed creativity. So one evening sitting around with Gary, I said, "I think I want to try again and build another brand." He looked me dead in the eye and he said, "Jo, I've been waiting for you to say that." That evening, we sat down with our notebook and worked out how we were going to do it. When I first started the second brand, I didn't know I was going to make it. And now honestly and truly, I feel like that thirty-year-old woman again living her dreams especially right at this moment. I am a person who believes that your dreams belong to you, and we all have a bank account of creativity. No one can touch that bank account but you. It belongs to you. No one can access it. But the only time it will increase in its value is when you use it. And then it can change the world. It can change your life and take you on huge adventures. That is exactly what has happened to me; I invested in that bank of Jo's creativity. I am glad I did it.

The following speech about the history of Hallyu was presented during a culture night program at an international youth conference. The speaker is a delegate from Korea. Hello, everyone! I'm Minsu Son from Korea. It is a great honor and privilege to be here today with all of you youth delegates from all around the world. Let's begin with a few pictures. Do you recognize these places? They are famous locations in Seoul. Interestingly, all of these locations also appear in the American drama XO, Kitty. The storyline of this drama unfolds in Korea. Isn't it surprising that an American drama is set in Korea? I believe this is a good example of the global fascination with Korean culture reaching countries all over the world. Since when did Korean culture start having a global impact? Today, I would like to explain the history of Hallyu by dividing it into four periods. Interest in Korean dramas and music began to increase in the mid-90s, especially in Asian countries such as China and Japan. In 1997, the Chinese major state broadcaster aired the TV drama What Is Love? According to the article titled "Hallyu in 20 Years, How Has It Changed?" from the weekly magazine issued by the Ministry of Culture, Sports, and Tourism of Korea, the drama achieved a viewership rating of 4.3%, while foreign dramas aired in China typically received around 1% viewership ratings at the time. The term Hallyu first appeared in this period, referring to the craze for Korean culture. Next, we find ourselves in the second period of Hallyu, spanning from 2003 to 2009. The year 2003 was a critical year as Hallyu set sail for Japan with the broadcast of the TV drama series Winter Sonata. During this era, Hallyu was also driven by many notable Korean idol groups rapidly expanding their global fan base, particularly among the younger generation. Fast forward to the year 2010. This time is remarkable because Hallyu began to reach a broader region over Asia and a more diverse range of people. This expansion was accelerated by the growth of new media, including social media platforms and video-sharing sites. Who can forget the "Gangnam Style" craze? Its music video went viral, smashing records by becoming the first to reach one billion views on a popular video platform, captivating people worldwide with its signature dance moves. As we approach the late 2010s, we find ourselves in the fourth period of Hallyu. The proliferation of Over-The-Top (OTT) platforms played a vital role in allowing viewers worldwide to access Korean content more easily. The influence of Korean dramas expanded beyond East Asia, making waves in Europe and South America. In 2021, Minari won the best foreign film at the Golden Globe Awards. This movie, infused with the essence of Korean culture, made a significant contribution to promoting the stature of Korean cinema on a global scale. With the rise in popularity of K-movies, everyday Korean dishes enjoyed by locals are now accompanying a global audience. K-pop artists sharing their meals on social media also sparked viewers' desire to try the same dishes. Consequently, various Korean dishes, including kimbap, Korean-style hot dogs, and tteokbokki, are now featured in foreign media. This represents a departure from the past, when traditional Korean dishes like kimchi, bulgogi, and bibimbap were the primary representatives of Korean cuisine. Korean webtoons have also become a global phenomenon. The Korean webtoon industry exceeded fifteen trillion won in annual revenue in 2021. According to the 'Global Cultural Influence Ranking' by U.S. News and The Wharton School, Korea has seen a big jump in its worldwide impact on global culture. Out of 85 countries, Korea has surged to seventh place in 2022 from thirty-first place in 2017. Then what are the key factors for Hallyu's success? In an article titled "K-Pop Groups Without Koreans" in Economist, the answer lies in glocalization. Glocalization involves blending global aspects from our culture with the local elements that are native to that culture. For example, platforms currently providing Korean dramas and movies provide subtitles and dubbing tailored to each country, so foreign viewers can enjoy them more immersively. Casting actors from other countries to create a story that fits the unique emotions of that country can be another example of glocalization. K-pop employs a glocalization strategy by fostering global groups through locally held auditions. Following local training, these groups prepare for their debut at the Korean headquarters. Hallyu's journey shows how culture can cross borders and bring people together with excitement. As we look ahead, I am hopeful that the future of Hallyu will continue to shine brightly and inspire us all. Have a wonderful evening.

❌ ④ desperate(간절한) : 간절히 사고 싶어 했다로 적절.

det.korean: 한류는 문화가 국경을 '넘어(cross)' 사람들을 하나로 모은다는 흐름이다. close(닫다)는 부적절.
det.analysis:
✅ ② close 가 부적절 — 문화가 국경을 '넘어서' 사람들을 모은다는 뜻이므로 cross borders(국경을 넘다)여야 한다. close borders(국경을 닫다)는 반대.
❌ ① fostering(키우는) : 글로벌 그룹을 키운다로 적절.
❌ ③ hopeful(희망적인) : 미래를 희망한다로 적절.
❌ ④ inspire(고무하다) : 우리 모두에게 영감을 준다로 적절.
det.tip: cross borders = 국경을 넘다 ↔ close borders(국경을 닫다).

det.korean: 빈 가방을 들고 다닌 거의 공짜 마케팅처럼, 최고의 아이디어는 '아주 적은 돈이 드는(costs pennies)' 것일 수 있다는 흐름이다.

❌ ① costs millions(수백만이 든다) : 이어지는 but(하지만)의 대비가 성립하지 않음.
❌ ② takes years(수년이 걸린다) : 비용이 아니라 시간이라 문맥에 안 맞음.
❌ ④ needs luck(운이 필요하다) : 본문 근거가 없음.
det.tip: cost pennies = 아주 적은 돈이 들다(= 거의 공짜).

According to the article titled "Hallyu in 20 Years, How Has It Changed?" from the weekly magazine issued by the Ministry of Culture, Sports, and Tourism of Korea, the drama achieved a viewership rating of 4.3%, while foreign dramas aired in China typically received around 1% viewership ratings at the time. The term Hallyu first appeared in this period, referring to the craze for Korean culture.

당신 말고는 아무도 그 은행 계좌를 건드릴 수 없다.
[조건] (1) account, bank, but, can, money, no, one, that, touch, you 중 필요한 단어를 골라 모두 사용할 것 (2) 정확히 9단어로 쓸 것

det.korean: '아무도 ~할 수 없다'는 No one can, '그 은행 계좌를 건드리다'는 touch that bank account, '당신 말고는'은 but you.
det.analysis: 뼈대는 'No one can(아무도 ~할 수 없다) + touch that bank account(그 은행 계좌를 건드리다) + but you(당신 말고는)'입니다. but은 여기서 '~을 제외하고'의 뜻입니다. [조건]의 money는 쓰지 않는 더미 단어입니다.
